Stanley Milgram. An American social psychologist famous for his controversial experiments on obedience to authority, which revealed a disturbing willingness in ordinary people to inflict harm when ordered by an authority figure. In the nineteen-sixties, Milgram recruited participants to deliver what they believed were electric shocks to another person in a learning experiment. The shocking finding was that most participants obeyed the experimenter's commands to continue delivering increasingly severe shocks even as the learner—actually an actor—screamed in apparent agony. The experiments demonstrated that situational pressures and authority can override individual conscience, a chilling insight in the shadow of the Holocaust and other atrocities. Though ethically controversial, his work profoundly influenced how psychology understands conformity, authority, and moral responsibility.

Born in New York, Milgram earned his PhD from Harvard, studying under Solomon Asch, a pioneer in conformity research. He conducted the obedience experiments at Yale University in 1961 and 1962, intending to test whether Americans would commit atrocities more readily than Germans, a question born from post-World War II experience and concern about what separates ordinary people from those capable of evil. He later taught at CUNY Graduate Center and died of a heart attack at age fifty-one, missing the full impact his work would have on psychology and ethics.

In Milgram's experimental setup, participants were told they were in a learning experiment designed to study memory and punishment. They played the role of teacher, giving shocks to a learner for wrong answers. As shocks increased in severity, the actor gave scripted protests—grunts, shouts, pleas to stop, then silence implying unconsciousness or death. When participants hesitated or expressed concern, the experimenter issued verbal prods: you have no choice, you must continue. The result was sobering: sixty-five percent of participants delivered the maximum shock of 450 volts, even after the learner went silent. Most were visibly distressed but obeyed anyway.

Milgram discovered several key variations that revealed the mechanisms of obedience. Obedience dropped dramatically if the experimenter was absent or gave orders remotely, a distance effect showing that physical presence mattered. Yet obedience remained high even when participants could see the learner's agony—spatial proximity did not override obedience to the experimenter. Obedience decreased when peers modeled disobedience or when participants had to physically hold the learner's hand on a shock plate. Importantly, obedience was not predicted by personality measures. The authoritarian personality was not the sole determinant of who obeyed.

Beyond the obedience experiments, Milgram researched the small-world phenomenon, showing that people are connected through a surprisingly small number of social links—foundational to understanding social networks and the interconnectedness of society. He theorized cognitive overload: people in urban environments process so much information that they become desensitized and less likely to help strangers in distress.

Milgram's obedience experiments became among the most famous and ethically fraught in psychology's history. They answered a pressing post-Holocaust question with a deeply uncomfortable answer: ordinary people will inflict pain on strangers if an authority figure orders them to do so and claims responsibility. This was not sadism or evil but obedience, the subordination of personal conscience to role and authority. The insight suggested that atrocities emerge not from pathology but from normal psychology in abnormal situations. However, Milgram's methods became a watershed for ethical constraints on research. Participants were deceived about the true nature of the study, exposed to psychological distress, and unable to truly withdraw from it. His work catalyzed the development of institutional review boards and informed-consent protocols. The controversy persists about whether his deception was justified by the insights gained. Milgram demonstrated the self-reflective power of experimental psychology: by showing people how readily they would obey, the experiments became commentaries on human nature and moral fragility.
